title: Laodicea (Revelation 3:14–22)
hookLine: lukewarm; and yet: behold, I stand at the door and knock

cards: A bath, run and then forgotten for an hour. You step in and flinch. Not hot enough to comfort, not cold enough to refresh.
Just lukewarm. The seventh letter in Revelation, to the church of the Laodiceans, reaches for exactly that picture, and doesn't soften it. But stay to the end.
Right after the hard words comes a quiet picture: someone standing outside a door, knocking, waiting to be let in for supper.

teach.b: First, the verdict: "I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot. So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth."
Readers hear this two ways. Some take hot and cold as passion and refusal: a complaint about half-heartedness.
Others hear water: hot water that heals, cold water that refreshes, lukewarm water good for neither; some link it to the water supply around the city.

teach.h: I AM RICH, AND HAVE NEED OF NOTHING.
teach.b: Second, how the church saw itself: "I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing." How the letter sees it: "wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked."
So the counsel: buy gold tried in the fire, white clothes to cover them, and salve for their eyes, "that thou mayest see."

teach.h: AS MANY AS I LOVE, I REBUKE.
teach.b: Third, why say any of this: "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent." The hard words come from love, the letter says, not from contempt.

teach.h: I STAND AT THE DOOR, AND KNOCK.
teach.b: Fourth, the knock: "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me." Sup means share supper.

Notice where the speaker stands: outside a door, asking to come in. Some preachers use this verse to invite one person to open their life to Christ. Others stress that it's spoken first to a whole church.
The words say "any man": the door opens one person at a time, and on the other side is a meal.

how: Revelation 3:20 is used in some churches as an invitation to welcome Christ personally, and appears in hymns, sermons and paintings of Christ knocking at a door.

o: the lukewarm church that thought it needed nothing
a church praised for its passion and its zeal
a church told to shut its door to strangers

games.q: the letter to Laodicea — tap the pairs.

s: Laodicea is scolded for being too cold
the letter says its hard words come from love
"as many as I love, I rebuke and chasten."
in the picture, Christ is already inside at the table
he stands at the door and knocks, waiting to be let in: "if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him."

games.q: you've just told a church it's lukewarm and blind to its own need. what's the very next picture in the letter?
o: a locked gate and a final goodbye.
someone standing at the door, knocking, waiting to share supper.
games.why: "behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him."

practice: Picture a door, and someone on the other side knocking gently, not hammering, waiting.

If you pray, say the verse slowly, "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock," then listen, and if you choose, open it; if you don't pray, let it be a door you've kept shut on someone, a call not returned, a friend held at arm's length, and picture your hand on the handle.
You don't have to decide anything yet; just notice the knock.

wordCard.voice: Laodicea. The lukewarm church that thought it needed nothing, rebuked out of love, with Christ outside its door, knocking.

orig.note: Greek: lukewarm. the word in Revelation 3:16.

carryVoice: Your line: I stand at the door. Hard words, and then an offer of supper. See you tomorrow.
